Elements of each group of the periodic table generally have the same electron 
configuration for their outer energy levels. Going down a group, the atomic 
radius increases, so the outer electrons move further away from the nucleus. 
In addition, the shielding effect of the core electrons increases faster than the 
nuclear charge. Both factors reduce the ionization energy of heavier elements 
in comparison with their lighter analogues.

1.4 The mole concept 
The Sl unit for amount of substance (n) is the mole, which is abbreviated to 
mol. One mole contains 6.02 x 1073 elementary entities. This number is the 
fixed numerical value of the Avogadro constant, N,. 
The mole applies to any species, such as atoms, molecules, ions or electrons. 
The masses of atoms and molecules are very small, so they are commonly 
expressed as unitless ratios relative to the mass of the 2C atom, which is 
defined as exactly 12.00 on the relative scale. These ratios are known as 
relative atomic mass (Ar) and relative formula mass (Ml), respectively. Relative 
formula mass of a molecule is also known as relative molecular mass. 
* The amount of substance, n, is the number of atoms, molecules or 
ions, expressed in moles, in a given quantity of the substance. 
* The mole (abbreviated to mol) is the S| unit for amount of substance. 
* The Avogadro constant, N, =~6.02 x 10®mol ™,is the number

The ideal gas model predicts and explains the behaviour of real gases in 
most practical situations. The key assumptions of this model are: 
* gas molecules are in constant random motion; 
» collisions between gas molecules are perfectly elastic; 
* the volume occupied by gas molecules is negligible compared with the 
volume of the container filled with the gas; 
* intermolecular forces between gas molecules are negligible; 
* average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to 
absolute temperature (in kelvin). 
Assessment tip

The behaviour of ideal gases is described by three laws. 
Boyle's law: pressure of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to its volume 
at constant temperature (p o :—/) 
Charles’s law: volume of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute 
temperature at constant pressure (V o T). 
Gay-Lussac’s law: pressure of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its 
absolute temperature at constant volume (p « T).
